sentences.text: - Anytime you sit down at a restaurant in the US, there's a good chance what you're eating came from Sysco.
Over the years, it's bought dozens of companies, building an $80 billion empire.
Now Sysco wants to make its biggest buy yet, Restaurant Depot, a low cost warehouse where chefs shop for themselves.
- On an average trip, I'm saving somewhere around 50 to $100.
- Critics say the deal could remove one of the few ways restaurants keep Sysco's prices in check.
To understand how Sysco got so big, we got rare access to its warehouses.
And the suppliers that keep them stocked.
Then we went shopping with the chef to find out why having another option matters and whether this deal could affect what restaurants pay for the food on your plate.
Sysco is known as a broadline food distributor, meaning it sells and delivers hundreds of thousands of products a restaurant might need.
Everything from frozen french fries to hand soap.
It sources these products from other companies like Buckhead, one of its specialty meat suppliers, which Sysco acquired in 1999.
Since then, Buckhead expanded from a single cut shop into 25 facilities across North America.
- Nobody in the building is a vegetarian, but actually our director of human resources is a vegetarian.
- Is that allowed?
- It is allowed, we allow that.
Anything that is a usable trim will go down into the conveyor belt right here, and that goes into these big mine carts that we'll pack off.
And those goes to cooking shops, right?
People that make frozen homemade meatballs at the grocery store that you get or hot dogs.
- Plant manager Dan Smith says these machines evenly slice meat like steak filets and tenderloins, so restaurants know exactly how many ounces of protein they're getting.
Laser beams scan a chunk of meat.
Then a computer calculates the maximum number of steaks it can cut from that chunk.
- It's gonna automatically adjust the belt speed to get the maximum number of driver portions that we're looking for.
- Another specialty inside this 28,000 square foot plant is dry aging.
- Some of the best steakhouses in the country are always gonna offer a dry aged steak because of that strong, unctuous flavor.
- But Sysco didn't stop after buying Buckhead.
A year later, it acquired FreshPoint, which supplies most of its produce.
Back then, FreshPoint had 22 locations.
Today, it has 32, making it the largest wholly owned fruit and vegetable distributor in North America, supplying Sysco with 750,000 pounds of produce.
Thousands of cases of watermelon, cauliflower, and tomatoes arrive at this Maryland plant every week.
It's 330,000 square feet, about six football fields.
Here, machines can chop up and package a head of romaine lettuce in just four minutes.
- We also do the exact opposite.
We're cutting peppers by hand, so depending on what our customers need, we adjust our process.
- The facility slices, chops, and packages roughly 3,000 different products, including grab and go salads and sandwiches and ready to grill veggie kebabs.
Getting all these goods to their final destination is a massive logistical challenge.
Before any Sysco product reaches a restaurant, it's trucked to warehouses like this one, which stocks more than 15,000 products for restaurants in New York City and New Jersey.
You've probably seen a lot of these brands before.
Markis Johnson is a selector here, someone who grabs up to 150 items and organizes them for shipment.
- I reference Tetris all the time.
And growing up, I used to love Tetris anyway.
I actually have Tetris on my phone.
- The hours are long.
Markis's shift can be anywhere from 40 to 75 hours each week.
- I'm fairly like slim now, you know what I'm saying?
But when I first started, I lost 14 pounds.
- Markis has to build the pallet carefully so products don't get crushed or leak.
- You have to think in here, but thinking too much will hurt you because everything is time-based.
Time is money.
- A fleet of delivery drivers trucks everything to restaurants.
Evan Berkofsky is transporting a pallet across New York City today.
- What's the weirdest thing you've ever delivered?
- Live lobster.
Yeah, because I honestly didn't even know we had that until there was, the box was moving and I'm like, what is going on here?
- He says he makes between eight and 14 stops a day.
Moving, lifting, scanning, and unpacking.
- And how many steps do you get a day?
- I'd say around 20 to 30,000 steps a day.
- But before truck fleets like this, most foods stayed close to home.
In the early 20th century, most restaurants and households got their food locally from suppliers like butchers, bakers, and egg farmers.
Then in the 1930s, refrigerated trucks made it possible for wholesalers to move food long distances while keeping meat, cheese, and dairy fresh longer.
So in 1946, John Baugh launched Zero Foods Company, a frozen foods distributor.
Seeing its potential, he teamed up with eight other regional food distributors.
In 1969, they officially merged to create Sysco Systems and Services Company.
Then Sysco went on a buying spree.
After gobbling up Buckhead and FreshPoint, it bought Brakes, one of Europe's biggest food distributors in 2016.
Then in 2021, Greco & Sons, a major Italian specialty distributor.
Over the decades, Sysco built about 40 private label brands.
These products are made by outside suppliers, but sold under names that Sysco owns.
Together, they generate more than $20 billion in annual revenue, and Sysco might be getting even bigger.
In March 2026, it announced it was going to buy Jetro Restaurant Depot for $29.1 billion, by far the largest acquisition in the company's history.
It's known as a cash and carry business.
Chefs physically go there, load up their cart, and buy what they need to run their restaurants.
To understand why Restaurant Depot is so popular and what its acquisition could change, we joined chef Rick Lee as he shopped for supplies for his New Jersey restaurant, Xina.
- You can get wares, you can get like a blender, you can get bleach, you can get a side of beef, all in one.
As you're walking through the aisles, it's a lot easier to be able to spot it than to scroll through pages that you're not even specifically looking for.
You get to actually see and touch the products before you buy them.
It's just like going to a grocery store.
- That in-person model isn't just convenient, it can be more profitable too.
Unlike Sysco, Restaurant Depot doesn't need a fleet of trucks and drivers to deliver every order.
Customers do the shopping and the hauling themselves.
For chefs like Rick, going to Restaurant Depot can also mean avoiding delivery fees, fuel surcharges, and other costs that come with ordering from a distributor.
- But you know, then you have to fill your car with 400 pounds of chicken.
Not necessarily ideal, but that's why we try to get things that are a little bit easier to handle.
- Restaurant Depot gives restaurants something else, leverage.
They can shop there as an alternative when Sysco's prices rise or when the products aren't up to standard.
According to Erika Polmar, co-founder of the Independent Restaurant Coalition, that could disappear if Sysco buys the company.
- Let's just say you're really frustrated that the strawberries that you're getting from Sysco are coming off the truck moldy and you complain to your Sysco rep and you say, all right, enough.
I'm gonna buy them from the local farm or I'm gonna buy them from Restaurant Depot.
And the Sysco rep says, wait, I don't want to lose your business.
Let me do this for you.
- But this isn't the first time Sysco has tried acquiring a competitor.
Back in 2013, it tried to buy rival broadline distributor US Foods.
The FTC sued saying the deal would reduce competition.
At the time, Sysco argued restaurants would still have other places to buy food because of cash and carry stores like Restaurant Depot.
But a federal judge sided with the FTC and halted the merger.
Sysco and US Foods later called it off.
- They said that the very existence of Restaurant Depot proved that there was competition in the market.
Now they're buying their competition and telling us that it doesn't matter.
- But Sysco says Restaurant Depot has a different business model and serves different customer needs.
It says the merger will maintain healthy competition while giving customers more options.
Sysco also told us it isn't planning to raise prices if the deal is approved.
- We will not be raising prices to Restaurant Depot through this acquisition.
- Brenna says that with Sysco's resources, they can expand Restaurant Depot as they've done with suppliers such as Buckhead.
- We can utilize our supply chain, our warehouses to bring that product through and our infrastructure to be able to open up a store.
That's gonna bring even more value to the communities.
- Today, Sysco supplies approximately 670,000 customer locations worldwide, including restaurants, hospitals, schools, and hotels.
More than half of Sysco's revenue comes from American eateries.
- Where are you visiting from?
- Wisconsin.
- Welcome, welcome.

- For restaurant chains with multiple locations, Sysco's size can make it easier to keep every kitchen stocked, like Carnegie Diner, which operates seven locations across the US, serving thousands of customers every day.
- Sysco is providing right now almost 90% of our food product.
- CEO Stathis Antonakopoulos plans to open four more.
- It's about the sourcing of the ingredients, the freshness, and how likable it is right now, or how we like to call it, how Instagrammable is now.
If we don't have all those four things, then a plate doesn't make it on our menu, and Sysco helps us that.
- The restaurant orders up to eight pallets of products from Sysco's warehouses multiple times a week.
His kitchen managers can place orders through the company's app in 15 minutes and track exactly how much they've spent.
- Right now, if I want to know how much I paid in beef in 2024, I can go to the app and see it on Sysco in seconds.
You cannot do that if you buy from Restaurant Depot right now.
- But there's a catch.
Sysco requires customers to meet minimum order sizes.
For a restaurant chain this big, that's not a problem.
- I don't even know what my minimum is anymore.
I think it's 20 cases, but we never have to worry about that.
- But not every restaurant operates at this scale.
- Tight space.
- For smaller, independently owned restaurants like Rick's in New Jersey, those minimums can be harder to meet, which could mean extra fees or not getting a delivery at all.
- So I can come in here and spend $20, but I can't just order, you know, six things from the supplier.
I have to order 30 items with like a $1,200 minimum.
- Brenna says Sysco can adjust a small restaurant's delivery schedule to help it meet those minimums.
For example, moving deliveries from once a week to every two weeks.
Additionally, Sysco says it has a program for small restaurants in larger cities with no minimum requirement.
The company also offers services to help restaurants order more efficiently.
- When I had only one restaurant, they invited me in the kitchen to help me develop menu items and show me and educate us.
I didn't have to hire a consultant.
- 32 ounce prime Tomahawk.
- At this test kitchen in New Jersey, Sysco employs foodies to develop menus.
- You could use this in the same vein you would your balsamic reduction.
- Today, they're working with Kevin Gilbert, executive chef of the Cloverleaf Tavern, on ideas for fall dishes.
- This is a pumpkin waffle using our Sysco pumpkin puree.
I'm using our Belgian waffle mix.
- I'm looking at the textures, the colors.
I'm seeing how balanced it is.
I think this is a pretty fantastic looking waffle for the fall.
Butter has the flavor.
Everything blends really well together.
The flavors are there, the texture is awesome.
- While Sysco foodies help provide the foundation for these meals, Kevin still weighs in.
- How much do you tweak what's put in front of you by Sysco?
- I would adjust it a little bit just based on textures and flavors within the restaurant.
And although I do like this, I want to kind of make it our own.
- Tasting is just one aspect of what goes on here.
Before Kevin actually orders the ingredients, he says he'll sit down with Sysco to look at packaging sizes and pricing to see whether the dishes make financial sense for the restaurant.
It's part of a larger strategy at Sysco.
Sell restaurants Sysco ingredients that can save prep time while still leaving room for chefs to make the final dish their own.
It works this way at the Cheesecake Factory, which makes all of its dishes from scratch, but still sources ingredients from Sysco.
Over at Xina, Rick says he prefers to come up with his own recipes and find fresh ideas in the aisles of Restaurant Depot.
- I grabbed the short rib because I was like, okay, this is gonna be something that I'm gonna try to work on.
It's not something we normally carry, but it's just the moment of inspiration.
- Sysco says the Restaurant Depot deal would give shoppers more products to choose from.
- If you talk to the Restaurant Depot folks, that's one of the things they're most excited about.
How do we get fresh cut produce into their stores?
How do we think about vacuum sealed, cut steaks into their stores?
Things that they don't have access to right now is something that we can bring to them.
- Back in his kitchen, Rick is turning that inspiration into new specials, including a bone-in veal katsu.
- And then we're gonna use the lobster bisque for our lobster dumplings, and then we're gonna use our burrata for our scallion pancake dish.
- For Rick, Restaurant Depot gives him another option when Sysco's prices, order minimums, or products don't work for his restaurant.
Regulators will decide whether the deal goes through in the next few months.
For restaurants like Xina, the question is whether they'll still have the choice afterwards.
- When you have all these birthday parties that are like, you know, 10, 12 people and this comes out, they're gonna be like, I need that.
You get 100% upsell to things like this without any hesitation.

Qua nhiều năm, hãng đã mua hàng chục công ty, xây dựng một đế chế trị giá 80 tỷ đô la.
Giờ Sysco muốn thực hiện thương vụ lớn nhất từ trước đến nay, Restaurant Depot, một kho giá rẻ nơi các đầu bếp tự đi mua hàng.
- Trung bình mỗi chuyến, tôi tiết kiệm được khoảng 50 đến 100 đô la.

Để hiểu Sysco lớn mạnh thế nào, chúng tôi được tiếp cận hiếm có vào các kho của hãng.

Sysco được biết đến là nhà phân phối thực phẩm đa ngành, nghĩa là hãng bán và giao hàng trăm nghìn sản phẩm mà một nhà hàng có thể cần.

- Nó sẽ tự động điều chỉnh tốc độ băng chuyền để có số phần ăn tối đa như chúng tôi cần.

- Nhưng Sysco không dừng lại sau khi mua Buckhead.
Một năm sau, hãng mua FreshPoint, đơn vị cung cấp phần lớn rau củ quả của Sysco.
Lúc đó, FreshPoint có 22 địa điểm.
Ngày nay có 32, trở thành nhà phân phối trái cây và rau củ sở hữu toàn phần lớn nhất Bắc Mỹ, cung cấp cho Sysco 750.000 pound nông sản.
Hàng nghìn thùng dưa hấu, súp lơ và cà chua đến nhà máy ở Maryland này mỗi tuần.
Rộng 330.000 feet vuông, khoảng sáu sân bóng bầu dục.

- Chúng tôi cũng làm điều hoàn toàn ngược lại.

- Cơ sở này thái, cắt và đóng gói khoảng 3.000 sản phẩm khác nhau, gồm salad và sandwich mang đi, và xiên rau củ sẵn sàng để nướng.
Đưa tất cả hàng hóa này đến đích cuối cùng là một thách thức hậu cần khổng lồ.
Trước khi bất kỳ sản phẩm Sysco nào đến nhà hàng, nó được chở bằng xe tải đến các kho như kho này, nơi chứa hơn 15.000 sản phẩm cho các nhà hàng ở thành phố New York và New Jersey.
Có lẽ bạn đã thấy nhiều thương hiệu này rồi.

- Giờ làm rất dài.

Thời gian là tiền bạc.
- Một đội tài xế giao hàng chở mọi thứ đến các nhà hàng.
Hôm nay Evan Berkofsky đang chở một pallet qua thành phố New York.
- Thứ kỳ lạ nhất anh từng giao là gì?
- Tôm hùm sống.
Vâng, vì thật ra tôi còn không biết mình có hàng đó cho đến khi cái thùng cử động và tôi nghĩ, chuyện gì đang xảy ra vậy?
- Anh nói mỗi ngày anh ghé từ tám đến 14 điểm.
Di chuyển, nâng, quét mã và dỡ hàng.
- Vậy mỗi ngày anh đi bao nhiêu bước?
- Tôi nghĩ khoảng 20 đến 30.000 bước một ngày.
- Nhưng trước khi có các đội xe tải như thế này, hầu hết thực phẩm đều ở gần nhà.
Đầu thế kỷ 20, hầu hết nhà hàng và hộ gia đình lấy thực phẩm tại địa phương từ các nhà cung cấp như người bán thịt, thợ làm bánh và nông dân nuôi gà lấy trứng.
Rồi vào những năm 1930, xe tải lạnh giúp các nhà bán buôn chở thực phẩm đi xa mà vẫn giữ thịt, phô mai và sữa tươi lâu hơn.
Vì vậy năm 1946, John Baugh thành lập Zero Foods Company, một nhà phân phối thực phẩm đông lạnh.
Thấy được tiềm năng của nó, ông bắt tay với tám nhà phân phối thực phẩm khu vực khác.
Năm 1969, họ chính thức sáp nhập để lập nên Sysco Systems and Services Company.
Sau đó Sysco bước vào đợt mua sắm ồ ạt.
Sau khi nuốt Buckhead và FreshPoint, hãng mua Brakes, một trong những nhà phân phối thực phẩm lớn nhất châu Âu, vào năm 2016.
Rồi năm 2021 là Greco & Sons, một nhà phân phối đặc sản Ý lớn.
Qua nhiều thập kỷ, Sysco xây dựng khoảng 40 thương hiệu riêng.
Các sản phẩm này do nhà cung cấp bên ngoài sản xuất, nhưng bán dưới những cái tên Sysco sở hữu.
Cộng lại, chúng tạo ra hơn 20 tỷ đô la doanh thu hằng năm, và Sysco có thể còn lớn hơn nữa.
Vào tháng 3 năm 2026, hãng thông báo sẽ mua Jetro Restaurant Depot với giá 29,1 tỷ đô la, cho đến nay là thương vụ mua lại lớn nhất trong lịch sử công ty.
Nó được biết đến là mô hình kinh doanh trả tiền mặt tự mang đi (cash and carry).
Đầu bếp tự đến đó, chất đầy xe đẩy và mua những gì họ cần để vận hành nhà hàng.

Bạn được tận mắt nhìn và sờ sản phẩm trước khi mua.
Cứ như đi siêu thị vậy.
- Mô hình trực tiếp đó không chỉ tiện lợi mà còn có thể sinh lời hơn.

- Restaurant Depot mang lại cho nhà hàng một thứ khác, đó là thế mặc cả.

- Giả sử bạn rất bực vì dâu tây nhận từ Sysco bị mốc khi dỡ xuống từ xe tải, bạn phàn nàn với đại diện Sysco và nói, thôi đủ rồi.
